title: A Ember for the Choir
premise: Gideon Quintana, the last oath-bound swordspeaker, has spent her life in a valley where magic cannot follow — until the border wards collapse the same night the stars go out, and she is dragged into a country that officially no longer exists. Hunted by the Choir, a bureaucratic order that erased her people from history, she gathers a ragtag found family of exiles and ghosts to find the Door of Return, the only way to restore what was taken. But restoring her nation means unmaking the peace that keeps a million strangers alive, forcing Gideon to choose between inheritance and justice. In the end she forges a third path: she speaks her sword-oath into the empty sky itself, rekindling the stars as witnesses rather than weapons, and founds a new covenant that neither erases nor avenges.
about_author: Paloma Oyelaran is a former archivist who writes fantasy about the paperwork of empires and the people it forgets. She lives between two coastlines and insists both are home.

chapters.title: The Valley That Forgot
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. On the eve of the Oathfire festival, Gideon tends the valley's wards and buries another elder, feeling the weight of being the last swordspeaker. A stranger's lantern appears at the border stones. The beat is quiet dread: tradition kept alive by one tired woman.

chapters.title: Lantern at the Border Stones
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. She meets Sefa, a runaway Choir clerk carrying stolen ledgers, who warns that the wards are failing nationwide. Gideon dismisses her — until the first star goes dark overhead mid-sentence. The beat is denial cracking into fear.

chapters.title: The Night the Stars Went Out
chapters.summary: Alternating Gideon and Sefa POVs. The border wards shatter; the valley's magic-dead silence floods with old power, and the dead elders' voices return demanding answers. Gideon's oath-sword wakes for the first time in decades. The beat is awe tangled with grief.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Says About You
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. Sefa reveals the Choir's census: Gideon's entire nation was recorded as 'dissolved,' its name struck from every map. Gideon reads her own family listed under 'assets forfeit.' The beat is cold fury born from ink and bureaucracy.

chapters.title: Leaving Is a Kind of Dying
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon performs the leaving-rites alone, since there is no one left to perform them with her, and steps past the fallen border for the first time in her life. The outer world is loud, lit by no stars. The beat is disorientation and stubborn resolve.

chapters.title: The Road of Borrowed Names
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Traveling incognito, Gideon discovers other survivors of dissolved nations living under assumed names, tolerated but never citizens. An old ferryman recognizes her oath-knot and weeps. The beat is the ache of being recognized after erasure.

chapters.title: A Choir of Quiet Men
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. Pursuers arrive: Choir auditors who dissolve things politely, with documents. Sefa bargains, lies, and burns her own credentials to buy Gideon time. The beat is loyalty tested against self-preservation.

chapters.title: The Inn at the End of the Map
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. At a lawless crossroads inn, the found family forms: Sefa, the ferryman's grandson Tam, and Vess, a disgraced Choir cantor who can still sing wards. They pool their fragments of the truth. The beat is wary kinship over bad wine.

chapters.title: Doors Are Just Promises
chapters.summary: Vess's POV. Vess explains the Door of Return: a threshold the Choir sealed when it dissolved the nations, reachable only where a true name is still spoken aloud. Someone must say Gideon's country's name — which kills the speaker. The beat is hope arriving with a price tag.

chapters.title: The Price of a True Name
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon volunteers herself; the others refuse to let her go alone, each confessing what they lost to the Choir's dissolutions. First real trust forms around a campfire under starless sky. The beat is grief becoming fellowship.

chapters.title: Audit in Ashfall
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. The Choir catches up in a burning market town and offers Gideon restoration on paper — her nation reinstated as a museum province, her people as exhibits. She refuses. The beat is temptation rejected with a drawn sword.

chapters.title: Vess Sings the Wards Down
chapters.summary: Vess's POV. To escape the audit, Vess unmakes the town's protective wards, dooming it to raiders, and cannot forgive herself. The group fractures over whether justice outside the law is just another cruelty. The beat is guilt splitting the found family.

chapters.title: Tam's Country
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. Tam leads them through his own dissolved homeland, now a quarry, showing them mass graves the ledgers list as 'land cleared.' Gideon swears a private oath over the stones. The beat is mourning turned into purpose.

chapters.title: The Cantor's Confession
chapters.summary: Vess's POV. Vess admits she sang the dissolution rite over Gideon's valley thirty years ago, believing it mercy. Gideon's rage nearly breaks the group; Sefa forces them to hear each other. The beat is forgiveness demanded before it can be given.

chapters.title: Where the Sky Remembers
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Guided by the last unextinguished star, they reach the Door of Return — a standing arch in a salt flat, sealed with chains of written law. Sefa begins unpicking the seals with her clerk's knowledge. The beat is trembling anticipation.

chapters.title: The Choir Comes Singing
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The full Choir arrives, not to fight but to negotiate: open the Door and the peace treaties binding a million living strangers unravel into war. They offer Gideon everything except an apology. The beat is the moral trap closing.

chapters.title: Two Kinds of Justice
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon realizes opening the Door restores her nation but requires a death — hers or another's — and that the Choir's peace was built on her people's grave. She refuses both options and reaches for a third: speaking the oath into the sky. The beat is clarity in desperation.

chapters.title: The Oath Spoken Upward
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, climax part one. At the arch, Gideon speaks her swordspeaker's oath not at an enemy but at the starless heavens, offering her life not as payment but as witness. The stars begin to relight, one by one, like eyes opening. The beat is transcendent defiance.

chapters.title: What the Stars Witnessed
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV, climax part two. The relit stars become legal witnesses older than any ledger; the Choir's dissolutions are voided by testimony no bureaucracy can strike. The Door opens without a death, and the dead elders pass through singing. The beat is catharsis earned, not granted.

chapters.title: A Country With No Borders Yet
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. The aftermath: refugees of every dissolved nation gather at the salt flat to draft a covenant with the chastened Choir. Sefa is asked to write it — the clerk turned author. The beat is exhausted, fragile hope.

chapters.title: Homecoming Without Returning
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon visits her valley, now open to the world, and finds it changed but breathing; she plants the Oathfire anew with Tam, Vess, and Sefa beside her. Found family becomes chosen inheritance. The beat is bittersweet belonging.

chapters.title: An Ember for the Choir
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, coda. Years later, Gideon trains new swordspeakers from every nation, and sends an ember of the Oathfire to the Choir's hall — not as vengeance, but so those who erase may tend what they burned. The final line names her country aloud, safely, under stars. The beat is peace as ongoing work.
